Oct 20 : Qualcomm will cut jobs globally in a "performance-focused reduction" following its annual employee reviews, CEO Cristiano Amon told staff in a memo on Monday reviewed by Reuters, with notifications set to begin in November. The cuts are part of an effort to build "a stronger performance culture" and address situations where the company "has consistently fallen short of expectations," Amon said. The memo did not say how many jobs would be affected, and Reuters could not immediately determine the scale of the cuts. Qualcomm did not immediately respond to a request for comment. It had about 52,000 employees globally as of September last year, most of them full-time. Its financial year typically ends in late September.

One of the world's biggest smartphone chipmakers, Qualcomm has been hit this year by a slump in consumer electronics sales as soaring memory prices weigh on demand in key markets. Its shares have risen just 1.5 per cent in 2026, compared with gains of more than 12 per cent for the benchmark S&P 500 and nearly 60 per cent for the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index. In its latest earnings report in late July, Qualcomm forecast quarterly profit below estimates and said revenue from Apple products would decline faster than expected, while signaling that growth in data-center and other non-handset businesses would more than offset the lost revenue by fiscal 2027. The company expects the majority of its chip sales to come from businesses other than smartphones in fiscal 2027 as it expands into the fast-growing AI data-center market. Amon said in the memo business priorities, organizational needs, skills and expertise would be considered in making the cuts. "As we have expanded the business, so have the competencies and skills we require," he wrote. "We must have the right people in the right roles so they can perform at their best and the company can continue to succeed."

Oct 20 : Hasbro raised annual revenue forecast on Tuesday, betting on strong demand for its digital games, including "Magic: The Gathering", ahead of the crucial holiday season. The Play-Doh maker has posted consecutive gains in its digital gaming segment over the past seven quarters, while an increase in sales of collectibles linked to Marvel, K-Pop Demon Hunters and Transformers have boosted demand for traditional toys. Revenue in its Wizards of the Coast and Digital Gaming segment rose 31 per cent during the third quarter, while consumer products segment was up 4 per cent from a year ago. The company's shares were up 1 per cent in premarket trading. The toymaker expects fiscal 2026 revenue to grow in the range of 7 per cent to 9 per cent on constant currency basis, compared with its prior forecast a 5 per cent to 7 per cent rise.

BERLIN, Oct 20 : Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) said on Tuesday that it was investigating the online publication of emails stolen by unknown hackers during a cyberattack last month. An AfD spokesperson said hackers had targeted a hosting service provider used by the party and apparently copied data from a small number of email accounts, most of which had not been used for years.  "The recent online publication of what is presumably a portion of this data is currently being investigated," the spokesperson said. "A preliminary assessment can only be provided once this investigation has been concluded." The spokesperson did not say how much data was stolen.

LONDON, Oct 20 : Britain's competition regulator said on Tuesday it was seeking to loosen Apple's grip on contactless payments by proposing that the company lower fees and remove technical barriers, helping rival services compete with Apple Pay. The Competition and Markets Authority said its proposals would result in "substantially lower access fees" and easier access to Apple's contactless technology, opening the market to competition from digital banks and other providers. The proposed measures are less onerous than those imposed by the European Union in 2024, which included giving third-party wallet developers free access. Since then, companies including Vipps, PayPal, Klarna, Curve and BBVA have launched alternative payment apps, the CMA said. CMA Chief Executive Sarah Cardell said the proposals would open the door to more innovation and more choice, as well as boosting Britain's important fintech sector.

Apple said it had already made it possible for developers to offer contactless payments in their apps through NFC, which allows an iPhone to talk to a payments terminal or reader, and through its secure element, which stores sensitive material such as card credentials and cryptographic keys. The company said this allowed developers to create products and services, including in-store payments, transit passes and event tickets, while ensuring users' sensitive data remained protected by the highest security standards. MILAN, Oct 20 : Smart glasses that resemble ordinary eyewear are under increased scrutiny from European regulators and advocacy groups, leaving investors questioning whether sales can keep booming as Ray-Ban maker EssilorLuxottica reports third-quarter results. EssilorLuxottica launched its Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses, capable of filming and recording, in 2023 and the market has grown rapidly. Global shipments of AI-enabled glasses jumped to 8.4 million units in 2025 from around 2.1 million in 2024, according to research group Omdia. EssilorLuxottica's Meta eyewear accounted for 81.3 per cent of global shipments in the first half of this year. When it releases its third-quarter results on Tuesday, EssilorLuxottica is not expected to give precise data on the value of smart glasses sales, but may provide an indication. In its second-quarter trading update, it said smart glasses sales nearly doubled compared to the same period a year earlier.

SOME GOVERNMENTS CONSIDER BANS The resemblance to ordinary eyewear has been a factor in the success of EssilorLuxottica's Meta smart glasses, and is in contrast to Google Glass more than a decade ago, whose bulky, futuristic design limited mainstream consumer appeal. But the design's discretion is troubling to regulators. Last week, the European Data Protection Board, or EDPB, which brings together national privacy regulators, said the devices facilitated covert recording, including of bystanders' conversations. Louis Larere, portfolio manager at French asset manager BDL, echoed that concern. "The fact that smart glasses include a camera, allow users to livestream and instantly share content on social media could become a problem," he said. So far Norway has taken the toughest stance among governments, saying earlier this month it planned a temporary ban on the use of AI glasses in selected locations. Australia said in September it was considering barring the use of camera-equipped smart glasses in government workplaces. In a preliminary, non-binding statement, the EDPB urged manufacturers to combine measures such as visible recording lights, sound alerts and notifications to nearby devices while recording. The authority also suggested limiting live streaming, automatically blurring bystanders' faces and using location-based technical restrictions in sensitive settings like hospitals or schools. PRIVACY CONCERNS MAY LIMIT ADOPTION Ross Gerber, CEO of California-based wealth management firm Gerber Kawasaki, which holds Meta shares, said privacy concerns and social stigma could limit wider adoption even though smart glasses still hold long-term potential. "People will make you feel uncomfortable if you wear them, and people feel uncomfortable wearing them because of this," he said, adding that his pair of Meta glasses was sitting unused in his garage. A Meta spokesperson said the glasses remain popular for music, calls and live translations. "They were built to be noticed which is why every pair with a camera has a bright light on the front that flashes when you take a photo or video you can share with others," they added. "It's important that rules protect people's rights while supporting innovation and consistency across technologies," an EssilorLuxottica spokesperson told Reuters, adding that the company is working to help consumers understand how to use the glasses responsibly and respectfully. Data regulators in Italy and Austria both told Reuters that they were investigating incidents involving smart glasses being used by pupils in schools, and France's data watchdog previously said it had received a small number of complaints. "Authorities should think about banning these devices in public spaces in a more coordinated manner," Kleanthi Sardeli, a lawyer at European digital rights advocacy group NOYB, told Reuters. Growing privacy concerns could pose a challenge for EssilorLuxottica and Meta as they seek to position AI glasses, which can be used for making calls and listening to music, as a potential future alternative to smartphones. "(Privacy concerns) are a risk to this category. We already saw something similar more than a decade ago with Google Glasses," Cedric Rossi, luxury and consumer goods equity research analyst at Stifel, said. Rossi said Meta's unveiling in September of camera-free audio glasses was a first step toward addressing regulatory and privacy concerns. However, he added that, without a camera, users cannot fully benefit from the AI capabilities the devices are designed to offer. Other companies, meanwhile, are still drawn to the category and Google, in partnership with Samsung, plans to release its Gemini AI glasses before the end of this year. Apple is also expected to release its own smart glasses. BofA analysts in a report this month assessed the regulatory risk as limited and that an outright ban was unlikely even if additional restrictions emerge, particularly in Europe.

TOKYO, Oct 20 : The Bank of Japan may raise its inflation outlook for the next fiscal year in forecasts due this month, as rising oil prices exert longer-than-expected price pressures on the economy, four sources familiar with the central bank's thinking said. Having just raised interest rates last month, the BOJ is expected to keep rates steady at the two-day policy meeting ending on October 30, unless the yen renews its slide that lifts import costs and broader inflation, the sources said. But the central bank will likely maintain its focus on mounting inflationary risks in a quarterly report due after the meeting, the sources said, leaving scope for another rate hike as soon as December. "Consumer price growth may stay elevated for longer than expected, though there's no big change in underlying inflation," said one of the sources, a view echoed by two other sources.

"Inflation pressures exist but haven't jumped, so there's little reason to rush," another source said on the timing of the next rate hike. The sources spoke on condition of anonymity as they were not authorised to speak publicly. The BOJ was not immediately available for comment. In forecasts made in July, the BOJ projected core consumer inflation hitting 2.5 per cent in the current fiscal year ending in March 2027, before slowing to 2.4 per cent the following year. The projections assumed that the pass-through of the initial spike in fuel costs would moderate from the latter half of next year. In new forecasts due this month, the board may slightly revise up its core inflation forecast for fiscal 2027 to reflect the pass-through from the recent, renewed spike in crude oil prices, the sources said. Any revisions will be minor with little sign that dangerous second-round effects, in which the energy shock triggers a spiral of sharp wage and price rises, are becoming embedded in the economy, they said. The board is likely to roughly maintain its economic forecasts projecting growth of 0.6 per cent in fiscal 2026 and 0.8 per cent in 2027, with robust exports of AI-related goods offsetting soft consumption, the sources said. The BOJ is unlikely to incorporate the expected impact of a two-year cut to a consumption tax on food items scheduled from April next year, as a bill to put the move into effect has yet to pass parliament, they said. FINANCIAL CONDITIONS KEY The BOJ raised its key rate to a 31-year high of 1.25 per cent last month, signalling its entry into a phase focused on preventing underlying inflation from overshooting its target and raising the prospect of tighter policy. BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda has warned that underlying inflation, or the broad price trend stripping away temporary, one-off factors, may overshoot its 2 per cent target on price pressures from the Middle East conflict, a weak yen and brisk AI demand. With underlying inflation having roughly hit 2 per cent, the BOJ will likely emphasise in the upcoming report its focus on anchoring inflation around its target, the sources said, a sign of its readiness to keep raising rates steadily. The central bank is also expected to maintain its view that financial conditions remain accommodative, suggesting further scope for rate hikes, the sourcdes said. Still, recent data suggests inflation risks are not heightening in a way that warrants a back-to-back rate hike. While wages will keep rising next year, a big jump is unlikely as government fuel subsidies moderate the pace of increase in this year's consumer inflation - the base for which unions negotiate pay with companies next year, analysts say. Corporate inflation expectations remained elevated but did not accelerate from three months earlier, the BOJ's "tankan" survey showed on October 1, taking some pressure off the central bank to follow a hike in September with another in October. Many analysts polled by Reuters expect the BOJ to raise its policy rate twice to 1.75 per cent by June next year, with respondents' bets on the terminal rate centering around 1.75 per cent to 2 per cent.

ZURICH, Oct 20 : ABB dropped nearly 6 per cent on Tuesday as market nervousness about the sustainability of investments in artificial intelligence weighed on the Swiss engineering company, which is a major supplier to data centres. Record new orders and an increase in its full-year sales guidance failed to appease institutional buy-side investors who were looking for more, analysts said, as AI-linked stocks fell more broadly. On South Korea's stock market, which has become one of the clearest measures of AI sentiment, traders sold heavily on Tuesday as concern mounted over rising costs. While European semiconductor stocks also fell, ABB shares fell more than peers. The stock, which reached its highest level to date of 89.14 Swiss francs ($108.13) in June, dropped to 70.72 Swiss francs on the Swiss exchange after the results.

LONDON, Oct 20 : Demand for safe-haven assets is strong as AI jitters hurt tech stocks, the Iran war continues and keeps energy prices elevated, while worries about high government debt loads persist. Yet traditional safe havens have not performed as well as expected this year: Gold sold off after the start of the Iran war as investors ditched top-performing assets given losses elsewhere. Government bonds, once considered one of the world's safest assets, are volatile. Here is a look at how some safe havens currently stack up. 1) LOVE/HATE RELATIONSHIP WITH THE DOLLAR

Breaking with last year's 'sell US' theme, the dollar has rallied since the Iran war started, up 4 per cent since late February. That has reinforced its role as a go-to safe haven at times of global stress. A strong economy, higher rates, and the US's energy-exporter status have helped. But factors that caused traders to question the dollar's long-term safe-haven status, such as a more than $40 trillion debt pile and policy uncertainty, have not dissipated. The dollar is also vulnerable to tech selling as it has benefited from record capital inflows into US shares on optimism over the AI investment boom. The dollar could be nearing the back end of a bull market, Societe Generale chief FX strategist Kit Juckes said. "It hasn't got that much further to go," he noted, but said it was hard to justify a sustained bet against the dollar at present because the "big global story is that the dollar is a petrocurrency and we're in the middle of an energy crisis". 2) EUROPE WOBBLES, BUY SWISSIE One takeaway from France-driven bond turmoil is that the Swiss franc is a haven of choice when Europe wobbles. It is up over 2 per cent so far this month against the euro, poised for its biggest monthly jump since late 2023. "Concerns about France's public finances and election uncertainty in France and Spain have supported the franc," said Georgette Boele, senior FX & oil strategist at ABN Amro. She added that investors were also becoming less keen to use the franc to fund carry trades, preferring not to position against a currency with safe-haven qualities. Swiss rates at 0 per cent make the franc popular in trades where investors borrow in a currency with low rates to invest in higher-yielding assets elsewhere. The AI jitters should also benefit the Swiss franc, analysts said. 3) GERMAN BONDS A RELATIVE WINNER Government bonds' reputation as a safe haven has been battered by fiscal concerns. Borrowing costs from the US to Japan recently hit multi-decade highs. The tech-driven stocks selloff has, however, renewed some demand for bonds. There is another noticeable development. When US and French 10-year bond yields hit 24-year peaks earlier this month, German yields fell as their prices rose. Investors say that is a clear sign that triple-A rated German Bunds stand out as safe havens among major economies. Bundesbank President Joachim Nagel said Germany would remain the anchor of stability in Europe amid bond turmoil and was "getting fit" after years of stagnation. "Everyone worries about contagion in Europe and whether the Bund just gets dragged along with (French) OATs, (Italian) BTPs, so it's good that the Bund has acted as that European risk-off instrument," said Johnathan Owen, a portfolio manager at TwentyFour Asset Management. 4) DID YOU FORGET SHORT-DATED BONDS? Overall, high debt among major economies will continue to hurt long-dated bonds' safe-haven status, investors said. But short-dated government bonds provide some shelter because they are less sensitive to debt worries. "We really like short-dated bonds," said Rory McPherson, chief market strategist at Wren Sterling. "Because of all the concerns over debts and deficits, we haven't been buying longer-dated bonds." 5) GOLD KEEPS ITS SPARKLE Gold, another traditional safe haven, has had a bumpy ride. After hitting record highs at $5,595 per troy ounce in January, it fell after the Iran war started as investors tapped the precious metal, given losses elsewhere. Gold rallied again in August as inflation fears and concern that the Federal Reserve was not doing enough to contain price pressures returned. It is trading around $4,175. Central bank buying and safe-haven demand support prices above $4,000, analysts say. While high interest rates should limit gold's upside, a tense geopolitical backdrop and US fiscal worries should bolster the safe-haven metal further out. "In the longer term, gold should again benefit from continued strong central-bank buying and renewed concerns over US debt and its rising interest burden," said Julius Baer analyst Carsten Menke.

KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia has made no agreement or commitment to provide financial assistance to budget airline operator AirAsia , the finance ministry said, though it acknowledged concerns over the carrier's financial health following a jump in jet fuel prices. Reuters reported this month, citing sources, that AirAsia was in talks with the government over potential support. The airline's co-founder Tony Fernandes said the talks focused on aviation-related costs such as airport charges and fuel, not financial assistance In a written parliamentary reply on Monday (Oct 19), the finance ministry said it was monitoring developments in Malaysia's aviation sector, including recent quarterly losses reported by AirAsia that were attributed to rising fuel costs stemming from the US-Israeli war with Iran. The government was regularly engaging with aviation players and seeking views from industry and technical experts, as was the case for other economic sectors affected by the Middle East crisis, it said.

MANILA: Shares of fintech firm Mynt, operator of mobile wallet GCash, rose 1.7 per cent in its market debut on Tuesday (Oct 20) after the company raised 60.9 billion pesos (US$966.99 million) in the largest initial public offering on record in the Philippines. The stock opened at 6.60 pesos a share, in line with its offer price, before rising to 6.71 pesos. The broader Philippine Stock Exchange index was down 0.02 per cent. The firm's debut demonstrated investor demand for Mynt's payments business even as a broader sell-off in AI-related shares made investors more selective about new tech listings. "It is a record and, more importantly, a statement of confidence in Mynt, in the Philippine economy and in the strength of our capital market," Philippine Stock Exchange president and CEO Ramon Monzon said.

GCash users completed payment transactions worth 9.84 trillion pesos in the first half of 2026. BIGGEST IN THE PHILIPPINES Mynt's IPO surpassed Monde Nissin's 52.2-billion-peso IPO in 2021 to become the largest-ever IPO in the Philippines, according to data compiled by LSEG. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr said the listing came at a time when the stock market needed renewed investor interest and broader participation, adding that attracting fresh capital remained a challenge. He said strong demand from local and international investors offered a "reason for optimism" and reflected continued confidence in Filipino enterprises. The Mynt IPO attracted more than 20 cornerstone investors, who committed about US$500 million, or nearly 60 per cent of the base deal, according to the company. Investors included BlackRock, Citadel, Fidelity International and the International Finance Corp. Mynt sold 8.03 billion shares at 6.60 pesos each. The exercise of an overallotment option increased the deal size to 60.9 billion pesos from 53 billion pesos. Mynt plans to use the proceeds to fund growth in its digital financial services business, product development and general corporate purposes, according to its prospectus. Oct 20 : Oil prices advanced on Tuesday, with Brent hovering around a five-month high as traders priced in a geopolitical risk premium from Houthi attacks on Saudi infrastructure and reports of vessel attacks in the Gulf. Brent crude futures climbed 52 cents, or 0.47 per cent, to $110.07 a barrel by 0628 GMT, after rising as high as $110.70 a barrel in the previous session to their highest since May 20. The US West Texas Intermediate crude (WTI) contract for November delivery, set to expire on Tuesday, was up 0.36 per cent to $104.03. The more-active December contract rose 26 cents, or 0.26 per cent, to $98.80. "Oil prices remain well-supported ... This suggests the market is pricing in a significant risk premium, given the situation's volatility," ING analysts said in a note on Tuesday.

Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the claims and Reuters could not independently verify them. Also on Monday, a Houthi attack on a training camp for government security forces in Yemen's Shabwa province killed 58 people with more than 200 injured. The renewed attacks heightened fears about regional stability and underscored continuing risks to energy supply from the region, keeping oil prices above $100 a barrel. In the US, crude oil stockpiles were expected to have fallen last week along with product inventories, a preliminary Reuters poll showed on Monday. Friday's executive order by President Donald Trump waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs, including goods duties and penalties for purchases of its energy. However, Trump said on Saturday he had yet to announce a final decision on the matter, while Secretary of State Marco Rubio said officials wanted more time to evaluate the situation. Russia's crude oil production increased by 65,000 barrels per day in September to 8.43 million bpd, but remained about 870,000 bpd below that of a year ago, the International Energy Agency said last week.  "While the prospect of additional Russian diesel supply offers some theoretical relief, traders appear far more focused on the ongoing risk of further damage to energy infrastructure across the Gulf region," said Tim Waterer, KCM Trade chief analyst.
